notes: Thursday 19 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Wed 18 Nov (US/Europe). Economy: Anthropic record $81.3bn IPO; UK inflation 3.6%; Fed Waller wants half-point hike; record-low US pending home sales. Tech: Nadella on Outlook outage; AI mistakes Doritos for gun lawsuit; Nvidia Kress all-hands; GTA VI. Politics: Trump, Xi, Putin in Shenzhen; Jeffries nominated Speaker; Peltola wins Alaska; Israeli tanks cross Gaza yellow line. Literature (US): Supreme Court history books; Karl Kani memoir; Power Broker marathon; Jennifer Croft postcards memoir. Society: ICJ Rohingya genocide verdict; South Korea suneung AI cheating; overdose deaths fall; ICE flight contractor secrecy.

stories.headline: Anthropic raises a record $81.3 billion in the biggest stock debut ever
stories.dek: The maker of Claude priced shares at $83, above its planned range; trading starts Thursday on Nasdaq as 'ANT'.
stories.caveman: Anthropic, the company that makes the AI chatbot Claude, is selling pieces of itself to the public for the first time. This is called an IPO. It set the price at $83 a share, higher than the $70 to $78 it first planned, and sold about 980 million shares. That raises $81.3 billion, more than SpaceX's record IPO in June. The price would value the whole company at more than $1.4 trillion. Shares start trading on Thursday (US time) on the Nasdaq stock market.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a big test of whether investors still believe in AI after a rough few weeks, including Nvidia's CEO shake-up and a string of tech outages. Taiwan chipmakers depend on AI spending staying strong.
stories.camps: Fans see proof that AI is a real business; skeptics warn prices are bubbly and that a few AI firms now hold a lot of market risk. How the stock trades in its first days will be watched closely.
stories.image_alt: People walk past Anthropic and Morgan Stanley signs in New York

terms.explain: Initial public offering: the first time a private company sells shares to the public.

stories.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as petrol and diesel prices hit records
stories.dek: Fuel costs jumped 33.2% in a year because of the Iran war; energy bills are forecast to rise 26% in January.
stories.caveman: Inflation means prices going up. In Britain, prices in October were 3.6% higher than a year earlier, up from 3.5% in September and the highest in a year. The biggest reason is fuel: petrol and diesel cost 33.2% more than a year ago, the biggest jump since 2022, because the war involving Iran has pushed up oil prices. Factory costs are rising too. Separately, household energy bills are forecast to rise 26% from January.
stories.why_it_matters: When prices rise fast, central banks raise interest rates, which makes loans and mortgages more expensive. Oil shocks like this hit many countries, including Taiwan.
stories.camps: Some economists want the Bank of England to raise rates to fight inflation; others worry that would hurt families already squeezed by high bills and slow growth.
stories.image_alt: A petrol station price board in the UK

terms.explain: How fast prices are going up over a year.
The UK's central bank, which sets interest rates.
The price of borrowing money.

stories.headline: A top Fed official says the US may need a half-point rate hike to 'shock people'
stories.dek: Governor Christopher Waller says inflation is heading the wrong way and wants big action at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.
stories.caveman: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is America's central bank. It raises interest rates to cool down prices. Fed Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC he is 'very, very concerned' that inflation is getting worse and spreading. He said a half-point (0.5 percentage point) rate rise is probably needed at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, and the Fed should undo the three quarter-point cuts it made last year, maybe more. Markets already expect at least a quarter-point hike in December.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher US rates make the dollar stronger, which pulls money out of places like Taiwan. That is part of why the New Taiwan dollar is weak right now.
stories.camps: Inflation hawks say acting hard now prevents worse pain later; critics say big hikes could push the economy into recession and cost jobs. Waller is one voice; the full committee decides.
stories.image_alt: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller speaking

terms.explain: The US central bank.
Raising interest rates.
An official who prefers higher rates to fight inflation.

stories.headline: US home sales hit a record low as mortgage rates stay above 7%
stories.dek: Signed contracts to buy homes in October fell to the lowest level in 25 years of data.
stories.caveman: When people agree to buy a house, they sign a contract first; the sale closes later. In October, these signed contracts ('pending home sales') fell 4.7% from September and 16.7% from a year earlier, the lowest in the index's 25-year history, says the National Association of Realtors. The main reason: mortgage rates (the interest on home loans) are high, around 7.3% to 7.5% for a 30-year loan. Experts expect a slow winter for home sales.
stories.why_it_matters: Housing is a big part of the economy. When few homes sell, builders, movers, furniture stores and banks all feel it.
stories.camps: Buyers say homes are unaffordable; some sellers refuse to cut prices because they locked in cheap old loans. Lower rates would help, but the Fed is leaning toward raising them.
stories.image_alt: Aerial view of a US suburban neighborhood

terms.explain: A loan to buy a home.
Homes with signed contracts that have not closed yet.

stories.headline: Microsoft's Nadella admits a 'perfect storm' bug caused last week's Outlook outage
stories.dek: He says Microsoft should have tested better; the outage kicked off a week of failures across US tech, banks and flights.
stories.caveman: Last Thursday, Microsoft's Outlook email went down for huge numbers of companies. CEO Satya Nadella told CNBC it was a 'perfect storm': a hidden bug that only showed up under one particular pattern of traffic. He said Microsoft should have caught it in testing and built 'bulkheads' (walls between parts of the system) so one failure would not go global. That outage was the first of a rough week of breakdowns hitting airlines, banks, Apple and even the NSA.
stories.why_it_matters: Daily life now runs on a few giant tech companies. When one breaks, millions of people cannot work.
stories.camps: US officials say the outages are not linked and not a coordinated attack; senators want stronger protections. Critics say companies chase speed and AI features over reliability.
stories.image_alt: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on stage in front of the Microsoft logo

terms.explain: When a service stops working.
A mistake in computer code.
National Security Agency, a US spy agency for electronic communications.

stories.headline: Students sue after an AI camera mistook a Doritos bag for a gun
stories.dek: Four Maryland teens say armed police detained them; the lawsuit says over 99% of the system's alerts were false.
stories.caveman: Some US schools use AI cameras that look for guns in security video. Last fall at a Baltimore County high school, the Omnilert system flagged a student holding a bag of Doritos chips as having a gun. Armed police came and detained four students. Now the students are suing the company, the police, the school board and the principal. The lawsuit cites a state inspector general finding that more than 99% of the system's alerts in the county's schools were false alarms.
stories.why_it_matters: AI is being used to make safety decisions about real people. A wrong alert can put kids in real danger.
stories.camps: The company has said it is 'truly sorry' for the fear the families felt and markets its tool as reliable; schools say they want to prevent shootings. Civil rights lawyers say the tech and the adults both failed.
stories.image_alt: Police video screengrab showing students being detained outside a school
stories.image_credit: Photo: Baltimore County Police Department via The Guardian

terms.explain: An alarm that goes off when nothing is wrong.
A case filed in court asking for a judge to decide who is responsible.

stories.headline: Nvidia's interim CEO tells staff 'let's move forward' at first meeting since Huang left
stories.dek: Colette Kress held an all-hands with the new board chair and top engineers; some workers want Jensen Huang back.
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes the chips that power most AI. Its founder Jensen Huang resigned last week amid a scandal, and the board says it will not bring him back. On Wednesday, interim CEO Colette Kress held her first meeting with all employees. A person who was there told CNBC she said 'let's move forward' and talked about pay raises and yearly reviews. New board chair Harvey Jones and senior engineers joined her. CNBC also reports some employees are pushing for Huang's return.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is tightly linked to Taiwan: TSMC makes its chips and Huang was born in Tainan. Its leadership crisis moves the Taiwan stock market.
stories.camps: Supporters of Kress point to strong sales; others say Nvidia's culture was built around Huang. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress.

terms.explain: A temporary boss until a permanent one is picked.
A meeting for every employee in the company.
The group that oversees a company and can hire or fire the CEO.

stories.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI arrives, and critics call it a masterpiece
stories.dek: Rockstar's long-awaited game, set in a Miami-like Vice City, launches this week after years of hype.
stories.caveman: Grand Theft Auto VI is probably the most anticipated video game sequel ever. It is set in Vice City, a made-up version of Miami, and follows two main characters, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval. NPR's reviewer calls it a 'grounded love story, a gonzo crime thriller and a gaming triumph', praising its satire of American life and its huge, detailed world. The BBC reports critics broadly calling it a masterpiece. The PlayStation network had problems hours before launch.
stories.why_it_matters: GTA games are among the best-selling entertainment products of all time, bigger than most movies. Its launch shapes the whole games industry.
stories.camps: Fans love its freedom and satire; critics of the series have long objected to its violence and how it treats women and crime. Reviews this time are mostly glowing.
stories.image_alt: GTA VI characters Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval against Vice City

terms.explain: A new part that continues an earlier story.
Humor that makes fun of real life to criticize it.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin shake hands in Shenzhen before first-ever three-way talks
stories.dek: Xi met Trump at the plane; the three leaders meet Thursday at APEC for no more than an hour.
stories.caveman: Leaders from around the Asia-Pacific are meeting in Shenzhen, China, for APEC. Chinese leader Xi Jinping greeted US President Donald Trump off his plane with a handshake and a hug. Later Trump shook hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin, their first meeting in over a year. On Thursday the three will hold their first-ever meeting together, which the Kremlin says will last no more than an hour. Topics could include the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear weapons, trade and AI.
stories.why_it_matters: When the US, China and Russia talk, the results can affect Taiwan, Ukraine and global trade. Taiwan worries about any deal made over its head.
stories.camps: Some see the talks as a chance to cool wars; Ukraine fears a deal that rewards Russia, and analysts say just getting the meeting is a win for Putin. A Guardian editorial says 'it may be a first, but it's not progress'.
stories.image_alt: Trump shakes hands with Putin as Xi Jinping looks on
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via BBC News

terms.explain: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a yearly summit of Pacific Rim leaders.
Involving three sides.

stories.headline: Democrats pick Hakeem Jeffries to be the first Black Speaker of the House
stories.dek: The vote comes after Democrats won back the House; the full House votes January 3.
stories.caveman: The Speaker runs the US House of Representatives and is second in line to become president after the vice president. Democrats won back the House in the midterm elections, and on Wednesday they nominated their leader, Hakeem Jeffries of New York, for the job. The full House votes on January 3. If he wins, as expected, he will be the first Black Speaker. Jeffries said Democrats will focus on lowering the cost of groceries, gas, housing and health care.
stories.why_it_matters: The Speaker controls which bills get votes. With Democrats in charge, Trump will face more investigations and pushback in his last two years.
stories.camps: Moderates like his focus on costs; some progressives worry he is too cautious and want bolder fights. House Democrats have already told Trump allies to preserve records for coming investigations.
stories.image_alt: Hakeem Jeffries speaks at a news conference in the US Capitol

terms.explain: The leader of the US House of Representatives.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term.
The more left-wing members of the Democratic Party.

stories.headline: Mary Peltola wins Alaska's Senate race, the first Alaska Native ever elected to the Senate
stories.dek: After two weeks of counting, the Democrat beat Republican Dan Sullivan, giving her party a 56th seat.
stories.caveman: Alaska is huge and remote, so counting ballots took two weeks. Democrat Mary Peltola has now beaten Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The BBC says it is the ninth seat Democrats took from Republicans in the midterms, giving them 56 Senate seats and control of Congress for Trump's last two years. Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the US Senate and the first Democrat to win a Senate race there since 2008. She talked about families choosing between heating their homes and buying food.
stories.why_it_matters: Control of the Senate decides which judges and officials get approved. A Democrat winning in a state Trump won by 13 points shows how big the swing was.
stories.camps: Democrats call it a rejection of Trump's agenda; the race was messy, with court battles and claims of spoiler candidates. Sullivan had not commented yet.
stories.image_alt: Mary Peltola speaking in front of a US flag
stories.image_credit: Photo: Bloomberg via Getty Images via BBC News

terms.explain: The upper house of the US Congress, with 100 members.

stories.headline: Israeli tanks cross Gaza's 'yellow line' for the first time since the ceasefire
stories.dek: The army says it targeted Hamas sites; displaced families fled their tents in central Gaza.
stories.caveman: Since a fragile ceasefire last October, Israeli troops have stayed behind a boundary in Gaza called the 'yellow line', with Hamas controlling the other side. On Wednesday, Israeli tanks crossed it for the first time, rolling along Gaza's main north-south road. An army spokesperson said troops were targeting 'Hamas infrastructure'. Dozens of displaced Palestinians fled their tent shelters. A day earlier, the US-backed Board of Peace overseeing the truce said both Israel and Hamas were failing to keep their promises.
stories.why_it_matters: Any break in the ceasefire risks more deaths among civilians who have already lost homes and family.
stories.camps: Israel says it is acting against Hamas threats; Palestinians and aid groups say civilians pay the price. The move comes as Israeli politicians try to form a new government without Netanyahu.

stories.headline: Hot topic: books that show the Supreme Court was not always the 'final word'
stories.dek: Historian Rachel A. Shelden picks five essential books on the Court's political past, tied to her new book.
stories.caveman: Today many Americans think the Supreme Court has the last word on what the Constitution means. In a Lit Hub list, historian Rachel A. Shelden, author of The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, argues it was not always so. For the Court's first 100 years, ordinary people, Congress and political parties argued about the Constitution themselves. Her picks: Larry Kramer's The People Themselves, Jonathan Gienapp's Against Constitutional Originalism, Eric Foner's The Second Founding, Laura Kalman's FDR's Gambit, and Supremacy by Nikolas Bowie and Daphna Renan.
stories.why_it_matters: With fights over the Court's power in the news, history books on it are having a moment. Knowing the past helps people see the Court as political, not magic.
stories.camps: These picks lean toward critics of 'judicial supremacy'; conservative scholars defend the Court's role and originalism. A reading list, not a ruling.

terms.explain: The highest court in the US.
The idea that courts get the final say on the Constitution.
Reading the Constitution as people understood it when written.

stories.headline: Hot: hip-hop fashion pioneer Karl Kani tells his own story in a new memoir
stories.dek: The Brooklyn designer, son of a Haitian tailor, built a brand for 1990s rap culture.
stories.caveman: Karl Kani (born Carl Williams) started making clothes in Brooklyn in the late 1980s, inspired by his father, a Haitian tailor. Back then rappers wore big brands like Ralph Lauren and Tommy Hilfiger, but in their own oversized style. Kani believed hip-hop needed a brand 'from the culture', and he built one that dressed stars of the 1990s. He talked to NPR's Morning Edition about his new book, A Life by Design.
stories.why_it_matters: It is a story about Black entrepreneurship and how street culture changed mainstream fashion.
stories.camps: Memoirs tell one person's side; fans of '90s style will love it, while fashion historians may want more on the business deals behind the brand.
stories.image_alt: Designer Karl Kani walks the runway at Miami Fashion Week in 2024

terms.explain: A true book about the author's own life.
A culture and music style that began in New York in the 1970s.

stories.headline: Hot: 400 strangers read all of Robert Caro's 'The Power Broker' aloud in 66 hours
stories.dek: Lit Hub's James Folta drew a 3:10 AM slot at the reading marathon and loved it.
stories.caveman: Robert Caro's The Power Broker is a giant 1974 biography of Robert Moses, the man who reshaped New York City with highways and parks, often hurting poor neighborhoods. Last weekend, more than 400 volunteers took turns reading the whole book aloud in 10-minute chunks for 66 hours straight. Lit Hub writer James Folta, a big Caro fan, got the 3:10 AM Sunday slot and writes about the odd joy of reading it with strangers in the middle of the night.
stories.why_it_matters: A 50-year-old nonfiction book drawing 400 volunteer readers shows how alive Caro's work still is.
stories.camps: Fans see it as essential to understanding cities; some readers find its 1,000+ pages a slog. Either way, it is a cult favorite right now.
stories.image_alt: A reader at a podium at The Power Broker reading marathon

terms.explain: A true book about someone else's life.
A powerful 20th-century New York planner who built roads, bridges and parks.

stories.headline: New: translator Jennifer Croft's 'Notes on Postcards: A Memoir'
stories.dek: The award-winning translator mixes her life story with the history of the postcard.
stories.caveman: Jennifer Croft is an American writer and translator, known for translating Nobel winner Olga Tokarczuk. Her new memoir, Notes on Postcards, began in 2017 when she started reading about postcard history. Lit Hub published an excerpt: postcards were short and open for anyone to read, yet they became a way to feel close to someone far away. She traces their start to a postal conference in Germany in 1865.
stories.why_it_matters: In a world of instant texts, a book about slow, small messages feels fresh, and Croft is a respected literary voice.
stories.camps: Readers who like essay-style memoirs will enjoy it; those wanting a plot-driven story may find it quiet.

terms.explain: Someone who turns writing from one language into another.
A short piece taken from a longer book.

stories.headline: UN court to rule Thursday on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.dek: No country has ever been found guilty of genocide by an international court.
stories.caveman: In 2017, Myanmar's army drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority, out of their homes into Bangladesh. Survivors described killing, torture and mass rape, and villages were burned. The small African country The Gambia took Myanmar to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN's top court, saying this was genocide. On Thursday the judges read their verdict. Myanmar denies genocide and says it was responding to attacks by Rohingya militants.
stories.why_it_matters: A guilty verdict would be a first and would strengthen the 1948 Genocide Convention, written after the Holocaust. It shapes how the world protects minorities.
stories.camps: Rights groups and survivors hope for justice; Myanmar's military government rejects the case. Even with a ruling, the court has no police to enforce it.
stories.image_alt: Rohingya refugees who fled Myanmar in 2017
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via BBC News

terms.explain: Acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

stories.headline: South Korea's giant university exam is shaken by an AI cheating scandal
stories.dek: Half a million students sit the 8-hour suneung on Thursday after a top scorer admitted using a hidden camera and AI.
stories.caveman: In South Korea, one exam called the suneung largely decides which university you get into and shapes your future. On Thursday more than half a million people, mostly high school students, take it at 1,312 centers. The country even reschedules flights during the English listening test. But trust has been shaken: the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted cheating with a hidden camera and AI. The government has added emergency alerts and rewards of up to $75,000 for reporting cheats.
stories.why_it_matters: As AI tools get smaller and smarter, every country with big exams (including Taiwan) faces the same problem.
stories.camps: Officials say tougher checks will protect fairness; teachers' unions have criticized the response, and some say the real issue is a system that puts huge pressure on one test.
stories.image_alt: Students during South Korea's suneung university entrance exam
stories.image_credit: Photo: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters via The Guardian

stories.headline: US overdose deaths fall to a decade low, but the White House takes misleading credit
stories.dek: CDC data show deaths plunged; researchers say the drop began under Biden in 2023, before Trump returned.
stories.caveman: Fewer Americans are dying from drug overdoses, mostly from fentanyl. New CDC data show deaths are at their lowest in about 10 years, saving nearly 50,000 lives a year. The White House said the gains came mainly in the last 18 months thanks to Trump's border security and fight against 'narco-terrorists'. But drug policy researchers told NPR that the decline started in spring 2023 under President Biden, and most of it happened before Trump took office again.
stories.why_it_matters: Knowing what really worked helps keep the deaths falling; false credit can lead to the wrong policies.
stories.camps: The White House credits border enforcement; researchers say the decline began earlier and likely has several causes. Both parties want credit for good news.
stories.image_alt: Families look on as President Trump speaks at a fentanyl bill signing in 2025

terms.explain: Taking a deadly or dangerous amount of a drug.
A very strong man-made opioid behind most US overdose deaths.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the US public health agency.

stories.headline: ICE gives its deportation-flight contractor up to $305m without bidding, and hides planes from trackers
stories.dek: Records show ICE also added an FAA program that keeps CSI Aviation planes off public flight-tracking sites.
stories.caveman: ICE is the US agency that arrests and deports immigrants. It hires a private company, CSI Aviation, to run charter flights that carry people out of the country. Federal records show ICE agreed to pay CSI up to $305.7 million without letting other companies bid, on top of a new order worth up to $1.28 billion. ICE also changed the contract to use an FAA program that keeps the planes off some public flight-tracking websites.
stories.why_it_matters: Activists track these flights to know where people are sent, including to third countries. Hiding them makes it harder to watch for abuses.
stories.camps: The government says it needs flights to carry out immigration law; rights advocates say the secrecy and no-bid money reduce accountability. CSI says ICE decides who boards.
stories.image_alt: ICE agents prepare to board detainees onto a charter flight
stories.image_credit: Photo: David Ryder/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the US agency that deports immigrants.
